items.why: Explicitly contrasts the five men entering with the priest and armed men remaining at the gate.
Clearly tests the order of two different takings of the same objects.
The trees directly ask the thornbush to be their king, not ruler of the previously mentioned gods and humans.
The passage explicitly links their prosperity to the land lacking nothing.
A direct causal statement distinguishes the missing inheritance from Israel’s lack of a king.
The passage directly says Jotham lives there because he fears Abimelek.
Strongly distinguishes the relatives receiving Abimelek’s instruction from the citizens who are its audience.
The Levite leaves to seek lodging; Micah’s house is only where his journey later takes him.
The sequence is recoverable, but calling the mutual wish a request is somewhat unnatural.
“Does something” is too vague to identify the reported action naturally.
The reported field movement precedes and motivates the ambush, while the city departure is observed afterward.
It cleanly contrasts whom the mother says will make the image with the silversmith who later makes it.
The object of the servant’s attack is clear, though the distinction is quite easy.
The occupants die from the deliberately set fire, not merely from entering the stronghold.
Precisely distinguishes the duration of the priesthood from the separate duration of idol use.
The shouting immediately accompanies the turn, though being overtaken is also a plausible contributing prompt.
The fig tree’s stated reason is preserving its good, sweet fruit.
The specific purpose of approaching the entrance is to set the tower on fire, beyond merely attacking it.
The command explicitly concerns taking over the land rather than its inhabitants.
Micah expressly bases his expectation on the Levite becoming his priest.
“The residence the Danites visit” is an awkward circumlocution that obscures a simple route question.
The pronoun resolves to Jerub-Baal, but “the man” and “they” make the question unnecessarily vague.
Zebul is explicitly the secret sender, while Gaal is the person being reported.
Strongly distinguishes the priest they address from God, whom the priest is asked to consult.
The curse is textually last, but presenting it as occurring after the punishment blurs their close relationship.
Zebul clearly substitutes mountain shadows for Gaal’s claimed people, despite the awkward passive wording.
Jotham explicitly gives God listening to the citizens as the intended result.
The olive tree directly grounds its refusal in not giving up its honoring oil.
Micah’s wording clearly identifies his mother as the person who uttered the curse.
The cursing occurs while they eat and drink at the festival, after the grape work.
The passage explicitly attributes the lack of rescue to isolation from Sidon and other relationships.
